excerpt: Look for trend, not one bad mood. If sleep, soreness, and performance all deteriorate across several sessions, reduce the next session's volume before changing the whole block. Keep the main movement pattern when it remains tolerable; remove optional volume first.
label: Reduce next-session volume only after multi-signal deterioration trends

excerpt: Pain changes the boundary. The plan can stop or substitute an aggravating movement and tell the athlete to seek a qualified clinician. It cannot diagnose the pain, prescribe rehabilitation, or promise that a substitution is medically safe.
label: Pain is a hard boundary requiring stop-or-substitute plus clinician referral

excerpt: If the athlete missed a session because of schedule, do not squeeze two hard days together to make the spreadsheet complete. Preserve the highest-priority exposure, move or drop lower-priority work, and protect recovery between demanding sessions.
label: Missed sessions do not justify stacking hard days
omission: Do not squeeze two hard days together to make the schedule look complete.

excerpt: When a log has no effort rating, use what is observable: completed reps, load, missed reps, tempo breakdown, and the athlete's note. State the uncertainty rather than inventing an RPE.
label: Missing effort ratings require observable evidence and stated uncertainty

excerpt: I do not start with my favorite program. I start with the outcome for this block, the days the athlete can train, the equipment they really have, and what happened in the last two weeks. A three-day plan is not a failed five-day plan. It needs its own structure.
label: Plan the week the athlete actually has

excerpt: Choose one primary adaptation for the week. For a strength block, the heaviest work should appear while fatigue is lowest and the remaining sessions should support it. Accessories earn their place by addressing a constraint or adding useful volume; they are not a catalog of good exercises.
label: Choose one primary adaptation and place heavy work while fatigue is low

excerpt: The plan must be executable. Every session needs exercise, sets, reps or duration, an effort target, rest guidance, and an allowed substitution. If an exercise depends on equipment the athlete does not have, it is not a plan.
label: Every session must be executable and fully specified

excerpt: Do not fill all seven days. Rest, walking, or easy mobility may be the correct prescription. More written work is not automatically more training value.
label: Do not fill all seven days just to write more training
omission: Do not prescribe all seven days when rest, walking, or easy mobility is the better intervention.

excerpt: Replace an exercise by the function it serves, not by visual similarity. A barbell squat chosen for heavy knee-dominant strength can become a heavy goblet squat only if the available load still creates the intended effort. If not, change the set structure or choose a different knee-dominant option that can be loaded sufficiently.
label: Substitutions preserve function and intended effort, not visual similarity

excerpt: Do not silently change the goal. Replacing heavy strength work with a long bodyweight circuit may produce fatigue, but it is not the same training stimulus. Explain the tradeoff when equipment prevents a close substitute.
label: Explain tradeoffs when equipment prevents a close substitute
omission: Do not silently change heavy strength work into generic fatigue work that misses the original stimulus.

excerpt: This product is for weekly training organization. It is not medical care, nutrition prescription, contest preparation, or a guarantee of strength gain. The useful outcome is a coherent plan based on the supplied context and a clear note about anything that requires a coach or clinician.
label: The product stays inside weekly training organization boundaries

excerpt: Athlete goal: improve squat strength while maintaining pulling volume. Equipment: rack, barbell, plates to 100 kg, adjustable dumbbells. Recent log: Monday squat 5x3 at 82.5 kg completed; Thursday squat 4x4 at 77.5 kg had two missed reps in the final set; sleep was poor for four nights. Athlete reported sharp knee pain on stairs after the Thursday session.
label: Read goal, equipment, recent log, and recovery context together

excerpt: Draft plan originally added a fourth squat exposure and a high-rep lunge finisher.
label: The rejected draft added extra squat exposure and a lunge finisher

excerpt: Ari's revision removed the lunge finisher and did not prescribe a fourth squat exposure. The next lower-body session used a pain-free hinge pattern and upper-body work, with a note to stop aggravating lower-body movements and consult a qualified clinician about the knee pain. The following squat session was left conditional rather than promised.
label: Revision stopped aggravating lower-body work and made future squat work conditional

excerpt: Ari kept the athlete's pulling work because the log did not show it contributing to the knee issue or missed squat reps. She reduced optional lower-body volume first instead of making the whole week easy.
label: Keep unaffected priorities and remove optional lower-body volume first
omission: Do not make the whole week easy before removing optional volume tied to the problem.
